title: Google to Allow Third-Party Android App Stores After Epic Settlement Talks End
content:
Epic Games and Google have withdrawn their joint proposal to settle the United States lawsuit that is reshaping the Android app‑store ecosystem. The lawsuit, which has been litigated in federal court since 2021, seeks to compel Google to allow rival app‑store operators to run within the Google Play interface and to share Google’s entire catalog of apps with those stores. With the withdrawal, the court’s earlier ruling by Judge James Donato remains in force, meaning Google must now comply with the order.

Under the judge’s directive, Google is slated to begin carrying third‑party app stores on Wednesday, July 22. The move is expected to open the Android platform to competitors such as Amazon, Samsung, and other emerging storefronts, potentially altering the distribution landscape for developers and users alike. The decision also raises the prospect of major players, including Microsoft, launching dedicated game‑store services on Android, following the precedent set by the Xbox Game Pass for Android.

The court’s order marks a significant shift in the mobile app‑store market, forcing Google to broaden its platform and providing consumers with a wider selection of app‑store options. The outcome will likely influence how developers distribute apps and how competitors position themselves in the evolving digital marketplace.
summary: Epic Games and Google have withdrawn their attempt to reach a retroactive settlement of the antitrust lawsuit concerning Android app stores. Google told the court it is prepared to begin carrying third‑party Android app stores on its platform starting July 22, 2024.

The watch offers a full set of fitness features, including dual‑band GPS, IP68 water resistance, a four‑channel heart‑rate sensor, and 131 sports modes, while remaining compatible with iOS and Android platforms and supporting popular apps such as Strava and Apple Health.

Battery life is a standout, with up to 13 days on a single charge under normal use and still maintaining an always‑on display for two to three days before a recharge is needed. The CMF Watch 3 Pro’s screen and design have earned it compliments for both style and functionality, and it is priced roughly $20 lower than the screenless Google Fitbit Air. For users looking for an even more affordable option, the CMF by Nothing Watch Pro 2 is available at $39 on Amazon and offers upgraded GPS, a more accurate heart‑rate monitor, longer battery life, and a slightly larger screen, all while sharing the same app ecosystem and swappable bezel system.

In summary, the CMF by Nothing Watch 3 Pro delivers a rare combination of a full OLED display, extensive fitness tracking, and long battery life at a price point that undercuts many competitors. Its versatility in colors and customizable watch faces, along with the availability of a cheaper Pro 2 variant, makes it a compelling choice for consumers seeking a stylish yet affordable smartwatch.
summary: The Nothing Watch 3 Pro smartwatch is available for $69 on Amazon, featuring a 1.43‑inch OLED display, dual‑band GPS, and up to 13 days of battery life. It supports iOS and Android, offers 131 sports modes, and comes in four colors with customizable bezels.

title: Amazon Wetlands Emissions Exceed Climate Model Estimates
content: Methane (CH4) is a potent greenhouse gas whose concentration in the atmosphere has risen sharply in recent decades. Wetlands are the largest natural source of methane to the atmosphere, but large uncertainties remain about how much methane comes from wetlands and how these emissions may increase in response to a changing climate. Tropical wetlands, including those in the Amazon, produce substantial amounts of methane, but accurately estimating their emission sources and magnitudes remains difficult. One reason is the lack of measurement data, especially in the tropics, where extensive cloud cover interferes with satellite observations and ground-based measurements are sparse.
summary: Recent low-altitude flights have detected significantly higher methane emissions from Amazon wetlands than previously estimated by climate models. content: Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers affecting men worldwide. However, planning personalized radiotherapy in the advanced stages of the disease still requires more precise tools. Researchers at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) have now tested a novel approach. A combination of two diagnostic imaging techniques could pave the way for personalized radiotherapy. The results of the study have been published in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry.

title: Among young adults, alcohol-induced blackout are linked to more harmful consequences
content: Young adults who experienced alcohol-induced blackouts (AIBs) reported more alcohol-related consequences than they did when they drank similar amounts without blacking out, according to a new study. AIBs involve a period of amnesia while the person is conscious and interacting; they may not remember what happened. AIBs are linked to consequences ranging from embarrassment and hangovers to sexual risk and developing alcohol use disorder. Among college students with recent AIBs, one in three drinking days involves this type of blackout—perhaps in part because young adults often do not perceive AIBs negatively. For the study in Alcohol: Clinical & Experimental Research, investigators explored the role of social context (who people drink with) and location (where they drink) in the alcohol-related consequences of AIBs.
summary: Among young adults, alcohol-induced blackout are linked to more harmful consequences.

title: Researchers Propose Reforms to US Sentencing Guidelines
content: The U. S. Sentencing Guidelines play a pivotal role in some of the federal government's most consequential drug policy decisions. Two recurring themes have been the balancing—or lack of balancing—between drug weight and the defendant's role in the drug distribution enterprise, and the basis for determining which relative weights of different drugs should be treated similarly. In a new article, researchers suggest approaches to these questions that offer constructive steps without jettisoning the overall approach.
summary: Researchers have proposed changes to the US Sentencing Guidelines to address issues in drug policy decisions, including balancing drug weight and defendant roles in distribution enterprises. The suggested reforms aim to improve the guidelines without abandoning their overall approach.

title: New cell imaging method shines a light on blind spots

Until now, scientists lacked a reliable way to see many of these molecular interactions as they happen. Researchers at the University of Illinois Chicago have now developed a new imaging method that allows scientists to see previously hidden enzyme activities in small regions across the whole cell. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, open new possibilities for understanding how cells process information.
summary: New cell imaging method shines a light on blind spots.

title: Scientists Utilize Sound Waves to Guide Cell Formation in Vascular Networks
content: With the aid of physical forces—in this case, sound—it is possible to actively steer the formation of engineered tissue. For example, sound waves can be used to create functional vascular networks with blood vessel-like structures in vitro. Scientists at the Center for Molecular Biology of Heidelberg University have demonstrated this through their methodology for acoustic manipulation. The team led by Junior Professor Dr. Daniela Duarte Campos also defines quality requirements for generating complex vascularized 3D tissue containing multiple cell types that is relevant, for example, to biomedical studies.
summary: Researchers at Heidelberg University have successfully used sound waves to direct the formation of engineered tissue with blood vessel-like structures within a week. The team's methodology involves acoustic manipulation to create complex vascularized 3D tissue containing multiple cell types, relevant for biomedical studies.

title: Study identifies harmful immune response to Candida albicans in Crohn's disease
content: Almost everyone carries Candida albicans. The yeast colonizes human mucous membranes—for example, the oral mucosa and the intestine—usually silently, without causing any problems. The immune system learns early on how to deal with it. It develops specialized immune cells known as Th17 cells, which keep the fungus in check. What exactly these cells do in the healthy body, where they originate and why they can become harmful in Crohn's disease have now been systematically uncovered by a research team from the Excellence Cluster "Precision Medicine in Chronic Inflammation" (PMI) at Kiel University. The study was published today in the journal Immunity.
summary: Candida albicans commonly colonizes human mucous membranes without causing disease, and the immune system normally controls it with Th17 cells. Researchers from Kiel University have detailed how these Th17 cells can become pathogenic in Crohn's disease, findings reported in Immunity.

title: Philips Hue Essential starter kit reaches new low price of $79.99 at Amazon
content:
Amazon is currently offering a discounted Philips Hue Essential starter kit, allowing customers to purchase a bundle containing four white and color E26 bulbs and a Hue Bridge for $79.99, a $40 reduction from its original price of $119.99. This deal provides an attractive option for those looking to upgrade their home's lighting with Philips Hue's color-changing bulbs, which can display millions of colors and produce up to 800 lumens of brightness.

The included Hue Bridge enables users to control the lights remotely, create schedules, and set automations, as well as connect up to 50 lights throughout their home. Additionally, the Bridge allows for control through major smart home platforms due to its Matter compatibility. The bulbs in this starter kit can display a wide range of colors and tunable white light, with preset lighting scenes available through the Hue app for various occasions, such as movie nights and holidays. Users can also create their own custom lighting scenes.

While this starter kit is a budget-friendly option, it does lack a few premium features found in higher-end Philips Hue kits, including more precise dimming capabilities and guaranteed color accuracy across generations. However, for those looking to add colorful smart lighting to their home at a reasonable price, the $79.99 deal may be an attractive option, effectively providing two free bulbs compared to the standard two-bulb starter kit.
summary: The Philips Hue Essential starter kit is now available at a reduced price of $79.99, which includes four white and color E26 bulbs and a Hue Bridge. This bundle offers control over lighting scenes, scheduling, and home automation through the Hue app and Matter compatibility with major smart home platforms.

title: Google Images Homepage to Feature Personalized Image Recommendations
content:
Google Celebrates 25th Anniversary with Overhaul of Google Images Homepage

As Google marks its 25th anniversary this week, the tech giant is introducing a significant change to the Google Images homepage. In a bid to revamp the platform, Google is replacing the traditional blank page with a search bar, with a new "browseable" homepage that showcases a dynamic gallery of images. This immersive gallery, which is updated in real time, is tailored to individual users' unique interests, providing a more engaging and interactive experience.

The new layout, reminiscent of platforms like Pinterest and Imgur, features a collection of images that Google thinks users might like, eliminating the need for a search query. This shift in design aims to make Google Images more accessible and user-friendly, allowing users to discover new content and explore their interests in a more intuitive way. According to Google, the new homepage will provide a more immersive experience, with users able to browse through a vast array of images without having to search for specific content.

The updated Google Images homepage is expected to roll out soon, marking a significant milestone in the platform's evolution. As Google continues to innovate and adapt to changing user behavior, this overhaul is a testament to the company's commitment to providing a seamless and engaging experience for its users.
summary: Google is updating its Images homepage to display a dynamic gallery of images tailored to users' interests, replacing the traditional search bar. The new feature will be available in honor of Google Images' 25th anniversary and will update in real-time.

title: Physicists Confirm 20-Year-Old Theory on Quantum Entanglement
content: Future quantum computing will require correlations between distant modules—a feature known as distributed entanglement. Traditionally, such entanglement has relied on active control and repeated measurements. Now, physicists at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) have realized a fully autonomous method for distributed entanglement using a "quantum bath" of correlated light particles. Published in Physical Review X, their work experimentally confirms a 20-year-old prediction and could provide a new platform for applied quantum technologies.
summary: Physicists at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria have experimentally confirmed a 20-year-old theory on distributed entanglement, a crucial feature for future quantum computing. The team used a "quantum bath" of correlated light particles to achieve fully autonomous distributed entanglement.

title: Scientists Explore Hibernation as Key to Deep-Space Travel
content: Scientists are trying to recreate the biology that lets animals survive months without food or water, in hopes of making deep-space travel possibleLong-term space travel is bad for your health. Very bad. Being in space exposes humans to dangerously high levels of radiation; extended exposure to microgravity can damage a range of organ systems, including muscles, bones and eyes. Living for months or years in tight quarters can have severe psychological effects. The key to solving these problems could be a 250m-year-old physiological strategy that allows mammals, birds, fish and other animals to survive extreme scarcity by essentially going offline: hibernation. When they hibernate, animals almost completely switch off their bodily functions; they don’t eat, drink or move, and just as importantly, aren’t hungry, or thirsty and don’t seem to suffer from the cold. This remarkable ability could prove crucial in helping humans get to Mars and beyond – and could also help save lives on Earth. Continue reading...
summary: Scientists are attempting to replicate the hibernation biology found in animals that can survive without food or water for extended periods, with the goal of improving human deep-space travel capabilities. This strategy could potentially mitigate the negative health effects of long-term space travel, such as radiation exposure and psychological strain.

title: Australia to fast‑track datacentre approvals and create national AI office, says PM Albanese
content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced on Wednesday that Australia will become the first country to consolidate the economic, social, national‑security and environmental aspects of artificial intelligence under a single national framework. In a major speech, he unveiled plans for a new Office of AI within his department, tasked with coordinating policy, regulation and investment across the sector.

Albanese said the government will introduce streamlined approval processes for AI projects, including data‑centre development, to give investors greater certainty and to maintain public confidence as the technology advances. The office will oversee the rapid deployment of AI initiatives while ensuring that potential risks to privacy, security and the environment are addressed through a unified regulatory approach.

The move signals a shift toward a more integrated national strategy for AI, aiming to balance innovation with safeguards. By centralising oversight, the Australian government hopes to position the country as a global leader in responsible AI development while protecting its citizens and ecosystems.
summary: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the government will introduce faster approval processes for AI projects, including datacentres. He also said a new national AI office will be established to integrate economic, social, security and environmental issues, making Australia the first country with such a unified framework.

title: New Zealand's Will Jordan Breaks National Record with 50 Tries
content:
New Zealand Wing Sets New National Record for Most Tries Scored

In a remarkable achievement, Will Jordan has surpassed Doug Howlett's all-time national men's record of 49 tries in 62 Tests, taking his tally to 50 tries in only 56 appearances for the All Blacks. The 28-year-old wing has been making waves in the rugby world with his exceptional skills, effortlessly gliding around the field and leaving defenders in his wake. Jordan's impressive performance has not only earned him recognition but also set a new benchmark for aspiring rugby players.

Jordan's ability to consistently deliver top-notch performances has drawn comparisons to a high-performance sports car, with his devastating speed, exquisite running lines, and world-class anticipation making him a force to be reckoned with on the field. His remarkable achievement is a testament to his hard work, dedication, and natural talent. As he continues to break records and push the boundaries of what is possible, Jordan is sure to inspire a new generation of rugby players.

Jordan's record-breaking performance is not only a celebration of his individual achievement but also a reminder of the importance of media and marketing support in helping emerging stars get the recognition they deserve. With the right platform and exposure, talented athletes like Jordan can reach new heights and inspire others to follow in their footsteps.
summary: Will Jordan, a 28-year-old New Zealand wing, has broken the national men's record for most tries scored, achieving 50 tries in 56 appearances. This record surpasses Doug Howlett's previous record of 49 tries in 62 Tests.

title: Open-source Revenue Leak Prediction Tool for Web and Mobile Apps
content:
UT Austin Student Develops AI-Powered Tool to Predict App Issues

A sophomore at the University of Texas at Austin, Rashid, has created an innovative open-source tool called Rejourney aimed at predicting issues in apps and websites before they occur. Rejourney uses real user session recordings to identify potential problems, allowing developers to fix them before they affect a large number of users. The tool is based on machine learning algorithms and can process thousands of user recordings daily.

Rejourney was initially developed to address issues with Rashid's own campus freebie finder app, which grew rapidly but suffered from onboarding and UX confusion problems. After losing around 340 users due to these issues, Rashid created Rejourney to prevent similar problems from occurring in the future. The tool works by recording user sessions, relating them to critical conversion events, and analyzing the sequence of user interactions to identify potential issues. If a trend is found, Rejourney's Large Language Model (LLM) processes the user recordings to determine the likelihood of a negative outcome and outputs a report with suggested fixes.

Rejourney has already shown promising results, with one user reporting a 30% increase in onboarding after fixing non-stop issues found by the tool. The company has also broken even on costs with its first three paid users, allowing for further development and expansion. With a focus on cost-effectiveness and user privacy, Rejourney aims to become a valuable resource for developers looking to improve their apps and websites.
summary: Rejourney is an open-source revenue leak prediction tool for web and mobile apps that uses real user session recordings to identify issues before they occur. The tool allows developers to track critical conversion events and uses machine learning to analyze user recordings and provide recommendations for fixes.

title: Gold nanoparticle biosensor detects early liver fibrosis from tiny blood sample

title: New Study Finds Sun Exposure Boosts Health
content: Extreme exposure should be avoided, but we’ve gone too far the other way – enjoyed safely, the sun can have enormous health benefitsHigh summer has returned to the UK, and with it, the usual warnings about the dangers of sunlight and reminders to seek shade and cover up. After years of such advice, most members of the public naturally assume that the science connecting sun exposure to poor health is well established, so people are often shocked to learn that the opposite is true: those who spend more time in the sun tend to be healthier. A lot healthier. I know because I began researching the subject nine years ago after stumbling upon some studies – and I’ve stayed on the case ever since, now summarising everything we know in my new book, In Defense of Sunlight. It contains good news for many people: we don’t have to fear the sun nearly as much as we thought. In fact, most of us could benefit from a bit more exposure. Rowan Jacobsen is a former Knight Science Journalism Fellow at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and a media fellow at the Nova Institute for Health in Baltimore. His book In Defense of Sunlight: The Surprising Science of Sun Exposure is published this month Continue reading...
summary: Research indicates that moderate sun exposure can improve health, challenging the common belief that sunlight is mostly harmful. The article summarizes findings in Rowan Jacobsen's book In Defense of Sunlight, emphasizing that while extreme exposure should be avoided, increased safe sun exposure can offer health benefits.

She tells Ian Sample about her work mapping fungal networks on the remote Palmyra Atoll in the Pacific Ocean, and what the research reveals about fungi’s often invisible roleSubterranean fungi networks more than 100 quadrillion km in length, study findsSupport the Guardian: theguardian. Com/sciencepod Continue reading...

title: Moon's Water Mostly Chemically Bound in Deep Interior
content: After decades of analyzing reams of lunar rocks back here on Earth, the canonical view of the moon was that it was anhydrous; that it had extraordinarily little water. That all began to change in 2009 with new data from NASA's Lunar Crater Observation and Sensing Satellite (LCROSS) and the much-ballyhooed evidence of water ice in the moon's permanently shaded polar regions (PSRs).
summary: Recent studies suggest that most of the Moon's water is chemically bound within its deep interior rather than existing as surface ice. This challenges earlier beliefs that the Moon was largely anhydrous and highlights the importance of subsurface reservoirs.

title: Sheffield Man Wins Final Spot at the Open Championship
content:
In a thrilling turn of events at the Open Championship, a local golfer has taken the spotlight with a dramatic finish. Joe Dean, a Yorkshireman, overcame a challenging moment of self-doubt to claim victory by a single shot. Admitting to feeling the pressure with six holes remaining, Dean's perseverance ultimately paid off. His fiancée served as his caddie throughout the tournament, adding a personal touch to the golfer's remarkable achievement.

Dean's winning putt was a testament to his skill and composure under pressure. A 4ft shot that landed with precision, it was a crucial moment in the game. The golfer's previous experience as a delivery driver likely contributed to his ability to remain focused and composed, traits that served him well in the high-stakes environment of the Open Championship.

The drama surrounding Dean's victory has highlighted the innovative approach taken by the R&A, the governing body behind the tournament. By shifting the focus towards the Open Championship during its own buildup, rather than solely on other events, the R&A has successfully generated excitement and attention for the tournament. This strategy has been exemplified by the attention drawn to world No 1 Scottie Scheffler, who missed the cut at the Scottish Open but remained a key figure at the Open Championship.
summary: Joe Dean, a former Morrisons delivery driver from Yorkshire, secured the final spot at the Open Championship after a dramatic shootout. Dean's fiancee served as his caddie during the competition, which aimed to provide a more engaging conclusion to the tournament.

title: Neural Network Implemented in SQL
content:
A team developing the open‑source array database library Xarray‑SQL has announced a breakthrough that could reshape how geospatial and climate data are processed. While overseeing a Google Summer of Code intern’s work during a babymoon in Corfu, the lead developer added a `to_dataset()` method that enables a seamless round‑trip between multidimensional array data and a relational tabular representation. The feature allows every N‑dimensional array to be mapped to a 2‑D table, treating orthogonal dimensions as primary keys, which in turn makes common geospatial operations—such as regridding and matrix multiplication—expressible as standard SQL joins, group‑by aggregations, and sparse matrix‑vector products.

Building on this insight, the team leveraged Coiled’s geospatial benchmark suite to demonstrate that many high‑volume (≈100 TB) climate queries are fundamentally relational operations. They further extended the framework by implementing automatic differentiation on DataFusion’s visitor pattern, inspired by JAX, and showed that gradient‑based physics calculations could be executed entirely within the database. By reducing Jacobian computations to row‑wise operations, the work suggests that neural networks could be trained using pure SQL, taking advantage of relational databases’ logical‑physical separation to potentially scale training across thousands of GPUs.

The research was presented at DataFusion’s inaugural showcase and is now being explored in collaboration with scientists and engineers at XQL Systems. Interested developers can join the discussion on the project’s Discord channel (https://xql.systems) and view the full benchmark documentation on GitHub (https://github.com/xqlsystems/xarray-sql/blob/main/docs/geos...). The team’s findings point toward a future where relational databases serve not only as data stores but also as distributed compute engines for complex scientific workflows.
summary: A developer has successfully implemented a neural network in SQL, leveraging the relational database's capabilities to perform linear algebra and calculus operations. The implementation utilizes DataFusion's visitor pattern and JAX's autograd implementation to enable gradient calculations and neural network training.

title: YouTube Guitar Tab Parser Tool Released
content: I created a simple CLI that turns a YouTube guitar-lesson video into a PDF of the guitar tab. There are services that transcribe music from Youtube videos into tabs, but they never work well enough for me. Instead I'm taking a simpler approach. It downloads the video, samples frames, uses Claude vision to locate the tab region, crops every frame to that region, de-duplicates the crops by the bar number printed on each line of the score, and stitches the distinct tab lines vertically into a PDF. I didn't test it on a lot of different Youtube videos yet, so problem will arise for sure. Comments URL: https://news. Ycombinator. Com/item? Id=48898154 Points: 12 # Comments: 6
summary: A command-line tool has been created to convert YouTube guitar lesson videos into PDF guitar tabs. The tool uses computer vision to locate and extract the tab region from video frames, then stitches the tabs into a single PDF document.

title: Pixel 11 Rumored Colors Include Fuchsia, Green, and Black
content:
Google’s next‑generation Pixel 11 is expected to arrive in a palette of eye‑catching hues, according to a series of now‑deleted Amazon listings that 9to5Google uncovered. The screenshots show the base model in a hot‑pink “Fuchsia” (Hibiscus), a vibrant green “Moss” (Pistachio) and a deep midnight black dubbed “Midnight” (Obsidian). The listings also contain two sets of color names, both of which appear in the early Amazon data, suggesting that Google may be testing multiple naming conventions before the device’s official launch.

The same research team also spotted early Amazon listings for the Pixel 11 Pro, which feature a dusky green “Pine” (Olive), a frosty blue “Light Fog” (Fog) and a pastel purple “Sterling” (Frost). These color options hint at a broader strategy to diversify the Pixel lineup’s aesthetic appeal, a move that could help the brand compete in a market where design variety is increasingly important.

While the listings have been removed and no official confirmation has yet been issued, the details provide a glimpse into Google’s potential color strategy for the Pixel 11 family. As the company approaches its product launch window, analysts will be watching closely to see which of the rumored palettes, if any, make it to retail shelves.
summary: Amazon listings show the Pixel 11 in Fuchsia (Hibiscus), Moss (Pistachio), and Midnight (Obsidian) black. The Pixel 11 Pro is rumored to come in Pine (Olive), Light Fog (Fog), and Sterling (Frost) colors.

title: Shokz OpenRun Pro price drops to $109, matching January low

Shokz’s last‑generation OpenRun Pro is now listed at $109 on Amazon, Walmart, and B&H Photo, a $50 reduction from its original $159.95 price tag and the lowest it has been since January.

Unlike traditional earbuds that sit inside the ear canal, the OpenRun Pro rests just outside the ears and transmits sound through bone conduction. This approach is praised for its noise‑cancellation benefits on flights and in noisy environments, but the company notes that the open‑ear format is more suitable for outdoor workouts where situational awareness is critical. The current sale price aligns with the all‑time low the product has seen, making it an attractive option for athletes and commuters alike.

In summary, Shokz’s OpenRun Pro earbuds offer a blend of music enjoyment and environmental awareness at a reduced price point. The $109 deal across major retailers underscores the brand’s focus on providing a practical, safe listening experience for users who need to stay alert during outdoor activities.

title: DJI Mic 3 two‑mic kit discounted to $219
content:
DJ Microphones has released its latest wireless lavalier system, the DJI Mic 3, aimed at content creators who rely on smartphones and compact cameras for high‑quality video. While modern phones boast impressive imaging sensors, their built‑in microphones often fail to capture clean audio, especially in noisy environments. The Mic 3 kit addresses this gap by offering two transmitters, a receiver, a charging case, cables, and four windscreens, all designed to deliver studio‑level sound for solo or multi‑person recordings.

The new kit is currently discounted to $219 from its regular $259 price at major retailers such as Best Buy, B&H Photo, and Amazon. The receiver now holds 32 GB of audio—four times the capacity of the previous model—and supports 24‑bit and 32‑bit floating‑point recordings. A built‑in screen displays battery levels and connection status, while magnetic clips allow easy attachment of the transmitters to clothing or hats. Noise‑reduction features include two levels of attenuation and active gain control to tame sudden loud sounds. Each microphone lasts roughly eight hours on a single charge, the receiver up to ten, and the charging case provides at least two full recharges for the set.

With its expanded storage, improved audio fidelity, and robust battery life, the DJI Mic 3 offers a compelling upgrade for vloggers, podcasters, and field reporters who need reliable wireless audio. The current price reduction makes it an attractive option for professionals and hobbyists alike seeking to enhance their video production without significant investment.
summary: The DJI Mic 3 two‑mic kit is now $219, reduced from $259, at retailers including Amazon, Best Buy and B&H Photo. The bundle includes two transmitters, a receiver with 32 GB storage, a charging case and accessories, and provides up to eight hours of microphone runtime.

title: Two arrested after 1,200‑hectare fire in Fontainebleau forest near Paris
content:
France’s fire services worked through Monday to bring under control a blaze that consumed roughly 1,200 hectares of the Fontainebleau forest, a sprawling woodland area located about 60 kilometres (40 miles) southeast of Paris. The fire ignited on Sunday in the historic forest, which was once a royal hunting ground and is now interspersed with several small villages. Authorities reported that the flames spread rapidly across the dense canopy, prompting a coordinated response from local firefighters, police and emergency crews.

Police have arrested two individuals suspected of deliberately starting the fire, though motives have not been disclosed. The containment effort continues as teams assess damage to the forest’s ecosystem and surrounding settlements. Officials emphasized that the incident underscores the challenges of managing wildfires in the region, and they remain vigilant in preventing further outbreaks.

title: Fire burns nearly 1,000 hectares in Fontainebleau forest near Paris
content:
A wildfire erupted on Monday in the historic Fontainebleau forest, a popular recreation area located south of Paris, prompting the evacuation of nearby residents and visitors and causing interruptions to both train services and highway traffic. Firefighters reported that the blaze has consumed nearly five percent of the forest’s 25,000 hectares, and investigators are treating the incident as a possible case of arson. The rapid spread of the fire has been attributed to the region’s ongoing heatwave, the third of the summer, which has left vegetation tinder‑dry and temperatures unusually high.

Authorities continue to battle the flames while coordinating evacuation efforts and restoring transport links. The incident underscores the heightened fire risk associated with the current climatic conditions across France, as emergency services remain on alert for further incidents in the heat‑stricken landscape.
summary: A wildfire in the Fontainebleau forest south of Paris burned almost 1,000 hectares, roughly five percent of the 25,000‑hectare area, on Monday. The blaze forced evacuations and disrupted train and highway traffic, and authorities suspect arson as a possible cause.

title: Free Mac App WhatCable Reveals USB‑C Cable Performance
content:
A new utility for Apple‑silicon Macs is giving users a free, built‑in way to evaluate the performance of their USB‑C cables after the discontinuation of a popular $8 hardware tester. The app, called WhatCable, taps into diagnostic information that macOS already gathers about connected USB devices—data that Apple does not normally expose to end users—and presents it in a simple menu‑bar widget. By clicking the widget, users can instantly see whether a cable is capable of high‑speed data transfer, power delivery, or if it is limited or faulty.

WhatCable’s functionality mirrors the earlier handheld tester that identified “fast, slow, powerful, or weak” cables, but it does so without additional hardware and at no cost. The software reads the cable’s electronic identifiers and reports its specifications, allowing consumers to verify the quality of third‑party or older cables directly from their computers. The tool expands the utility of Apple’s own diagnostics, offering a convenient solution for anyone needing to confirm cable performance in a growing ecosystem of USB‑C accessories.
summary: WhatCable is a free Mac app that reads data from Apple Silicon Macs to identify USB‑C cable performance. The app displays whether each cable is fast, slow, powerful, or weak via a menu‑bar widget.

title: Infantino hints at 64‑team World Cup 2026 expansion
content:
The final week of the 2026 FIFA World Cup is now in full swing, with teams preparing for the knockout rounds as the tournament’s climax approaches. Amid the on‑field action, FIFA President Gianni Infantino has reiterated plans to expand the competition to 64 teams for future editions, a proposal that has generated significant discussion among football authorities, clubs, and national associations.

The expansion would eliminate the current third‑place qualification mechanism, thereby reducing the number of matches that determine elimination and streamlining the tournament’s structure. Proponents argue that a larger field would broaden participation, allowing more nations to compete and potentially enriching the global football experience. Critics, however, point to the increased complexity of qualification, the need for additional venues, and the logistical demands on host cities—including stadiums, accommodation, training facilities, and media infrastructure—that could strain resources and planning capacities.

As FIFA weighs the benefits of a cleaner, more inclusive format against the practical challenges of scaling the event, the debate continues to shape discussions about the future of the World Cup. The outcome of these deliberations will determine whether the tournament’s expansion will proceed, potentially reshaping the landscape of international football for years to come.
summary: FIFA President Gianni Infantino said the 2026 World Cup could be expanded to 64 teams. The change would eliminate the third‑place qualification and reduce the number of matches that teams lose in the tournament.

title: Citizen scientists reveal evolutionary origins of paternal care in harvestmen

The rapid, data‑driven study, completed within days, demonstrates how publicly sourced biodiversity records can accelerate scientific discovery. The findings reveal that maternal and paternal care have developed independently in harvestmen, offering new insight into the mechanisms driving parental investment across species. This work underscores the growing impact of citizen‑science contributions on global biological research.

title: Mycologist Leads Three-Day Fungi Workshop in Tasmania's Tarkine Rainforest
content:
A three‑day fungi workshop was held this week in Tasmania’s Takayna/Tarkine, the country’s largest cool‑temperate rainforest. The event, organised by the Tasmanian Mycological Society, brought together mycologists, ecologists and local volunteers to study the region’s diverse fungal communities. Participants, led by mycologist Alexis Buxton‑Collins, explored ancient Huon pine stands and surveyed the forest floor for species that play a critical role in nutrient cycling and forest health.

During the workshop, Buxton‑Collins reported a growing appreciation for the third kingdom of life among attendees, noting that fungi are “ecosystem engineers” that helped create the conditions for forests to thrive. Dr Alison Pouliot, a senior mycologist, highlighted that fungi predate both animals and photosynthetic trees, underscoring their foundational role in the ecosystem. The team collected samples, identified new species, and documented fungal‑plant interactions that support the forest’s long‑standing biodiversity, which includes rare freshwater crayfish and the legendary thylacine.

The workshop’s findings reinforce the importance of protecting Takayna/Tarkine’s fungal diversity as part of broader conservation efforts. By understanding how fungi shape this ancient landscape, scientists aim to inform management strategies that preserve the rainforest’s ecological integrity for future generations.
summary: A three-day fungi workshop was held in the Tarkine, Tasmania’s largest cool temperate rainforest. Mycologist Dr Alison Pouliot explained the role of fungi as ecosystem engineers during the event.

title: Lawyer Mark Lanier wins landmark lawsuit against Meta and Google over addictive design
content:
Mark Lanier’s legal team secured a landmark victory in a Los Angeles courtroom on 18 February, when the jury found that Meta’s Instagram and YouTube were “addiction machines” designed to harm young users’ mental health. The case, brought by Lanier on behalf of a minor client, Kaley, challenged the social‑media giants on the basis that their platforms were engineered to keep children hooked, rather than merely hosting user‑generated content. The ruling required Meta to address the addictive design of its products and to implement measures to protect vulnerable users.

The trial was notable for its unprecedented focus on platform design rather than content moderation. Zuckerberg’s appearance in court, surrounded by Meta‑branded eyewear, underscored the high stakes for the company. The jury’s decision marked a significant moment in tech regulation, echoing the historic tobacco litigation that forced industry accountability. It signals that courts are now willing to scrutinize the underlying architecture of social‑media services when they pose public‑health risks.

This ruling is expected to influence how other tech firms approach product design and user safety. By holding Meta accountable for the mental‑health impact of its services, the case sets a precedent that may prompt broader regulatory scrutiny and compel platforms to prioritize user well‑being in their development strategies.
summary: In February 2024, attorney Mark Lanier and his client Kaley secured a Los Angeles jury verdict that found Instagram and YouTube were designed to be addictive and caused mental‑health harm to children. The case marked the first time the tech giants were held liable for platform design rather than user content.

title: Researchers Develop New Method for Imaging Spintronic Materials Under Stronger Fields

For example, photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM), coupled with a magnetically sensitive detection mechanism.

title: Jannik Sinner powers past Alexander Zverev in four sets to retain Wimbledon title
content:
Top-ranked Tennis Player Defends Wimbledon Title in Thrilling Match

In a highly anticipated match at the All England Lawn Tennis Club, world No 1 Jannik Sinner successfully defended his Wimbledon title by defeating German tennis star Alexander Zverev in a closely contested four-set final. The match, which lasted three hours and 46 minutes, saw Sinner overcome a challenging start to emerge victorious with a score of 6-7 (7), 7-6 (2), 6-3, 6-4.

The decisive moments in the match came in the fourth set, where Sinner faced a critical 15-30 and 1-2 deficit. Despite the gusty wind conditions, which had been a factor throughout the contest, Sinner displayed exceptional mental toughness and serving skills. He delivered a series of crucial service winners to hold his serve and ultimately turned the momentum in his favor. This display of resilience and skill allowed Sinner to recover from a disappointing first set and secure his second Wimbledon title.

Sinner's victory marks a significant achievement in his career, cementing his status as one of the world's top tennis players. The Italian tennis star's determination and skill under pressure were on full display throughout the match, and his ability to adapt to the challenging conditions ultimately proved to be the deciding factor in his success.
summary: Jannik Sinner powers past Alexander Zverev in four sets to retain Wimbledon title.

With her newfound platform, Noskova aims to make a tangible difference in the lives of others, reflecting her commitment to using her success for the greater good.

As the tennis world continues to celebrate Noskova's historic victory, her dedication to philanthropy and social responsibility is set to inspire a new generation of athletes and individuals alike. By prioritizing the well-being of others over personal indulgences, Noskova is redefining the notion of success and cementing her place as a trailblazer in the world of sports.

title: Frozen Soils in Arctic Regions Display Unique Geometric Patterns
content: Hillslopes in Arctic regions with frozen soils can host a suite of geometric patterns, from circles and stripes to polygonal patterned ground. They can also have solifluction patterns, or markings left behind when partially thawed permafrost slips and flows down a slope. Solifluction patterns look like pairings of flat, terraced soil—like a big staircase—and rounded lobes of soil at the terrace's base.
summary: Frozen soils in Arctic regions can exhibit a variety of geometric patterns, including circles, stripes, and polygonal patterns, due to gravitational forces and unique physical processes. Solifluction patterns, formed when partially thawed permafrost slides down hillslopes, can also be observed in these regions, featuring flat terraces and rounded soil lobes.

title: Declarative Language for Tool Orchestration Released as Open-Source
content:
New Tool Allows Users to Write Custom Procedures for AI Agents

A small but significant innovation has emerged in the field of artificial intelligence, with the launch of Skillscript, a custom language designed to empower users to write specific procedures for their local AI agents. Created by Scott, the founder of Skillscript, this tool aims to bridge the gap between human intention and AI execution. The language was born out of a desire to automate repetitive tasks, such as running morning briefs, and to utilize local models for simple tasks, which can wander off course if left unchecked.

Skillscript is a text-based language that allows users to define named steps, variables, conditions, and tool calls, all within a bounded and secure framework. This ensures that users can trust the language and its output, without worrying about the potential for damage or unexpected behavior. The tool is still in its early stages, with a pre-1.0 version available for self-hosted use and MCP-native integration. While it has its rough edges, Skillscript has already proven itself to be a valuable addition to Scott's daily workflow.

As the tool continues to develop, Scott is seeking feedback on its language design and trust model. Specifically, he is looking for input on whether the language is too small or too big, and whether its shape is correct. Additionally, he is seeking to understand what would need to be in place for users to trust Skillscript on their own machines. With a growing community of users and contributors, Skillscript is poised to become a key player in the AI tooling landscape.
summary: Skillscript is a small, sandboxed language for writing tool orchestration procedures in a declarative format, allowing users to specify actions and conditions without interpretation by AI models. The language is designed to be minimal, with a focus on safety and predictability, and is currently available as a pre-1.0 release on GitHub.

title: Guardian probes £8.2bn AI datacentre's renewable claims
content: The Guardian’s global tech reporting team are investigating the impact of the vast datacentres being built to power the AI revolution. We spoke to them about how their beat has become increasingly offlineJournalists often use the term “shoe-leather reporting” to refer to the on-the-ground legwork that goes into covering certain stories. As the tech industry’s focus has shifted from screen-based realities to the physical world of colossal AI datacentres and social media harms, comfortable footwear has become more essential to a tech reporter’s job. Earlier this week, we published the Guardian’s latest investigation into the datacentres and energy infrastructures that underpin AI – revealing that an £8.2bn AI complex in rural Scotland has misrepresented its plans to be powered entirely by on-site renewables. “Our reporting is showing that you can’t simply wave a magic wand and have a datacentre appear,” says Aisha Down, who covers AI for the Guardian and went to Scotland to investigate the story. “There are a lot of huge physical constraints and reality checks. These physical, tangible things are what makes or sinks the AI boom.” Continue reading...

title: Local protests target AI data center construction
content:
A yard sign denouncing a proposed data‑center project has been erected along Route 54 in Mount Carmel Township, Northumberland County, signaling local resistance to the development. The sign, captured by Getty Images, joins a growing number of community‑level actions that have emerged as municipalities across the United States confront the infrastructure demands of expanding digital services. The controversy is highlighted in this week’s edition of The Stepback, a newsletter that distills a single tech‑industry story for subscribers each Sunday at 8 a.m. ET, with additional coverage provided by reporter Emma Roth.

The Mount Carmel dispute echoes earlier opposition movements, such as the 2015 protest against Apple’s plan to construct a roughly $1 billion, 500‑acre data center in Athenry, Ireland, intended to power European services like iTunes, iMessage and Siri. Those early demonstrations foreshadowed the current wave of community concerns over power‑grid strain and environmental impact associated with large‑scale data facilities. As the Mount Carmel case unfolds, it adds to a broader dialogue about balancing technological growth with local resource capacity and public sentiment.
summary: Residents displayed a yard sign opposing a planned AI data center along Route 54 in Mount Carmel Township, Northumberland County. The opposition follows earlier resistance to large data center projects, including Apple’s 2015 announcement of a $1 billion facility in Athenry, Ireland.

title: Argentina defeat Switzerland 2-1 in extra time to reach World Cup semi‑finals
content:
Argentina’s quarter‑final clash with Switzerland proved a microcosm of the rollercoaster journey the Argentine side must endure to lift the World Cup trophy. What began as a seemingly straightforward encounter quickly turned into a tense battle, with the hosts threatening to squander their chances before a moment of brilliance salvaged the result. The match extended into extra time, and the Argentine squad found themselves on the brink of a penalty shoot‑out when Lionel Messi was denied by Swiss goalkeeper Gregor Kobel.

In the second period of extra time, a decisive thunderbolt changed the course of the game. After a well‑timed pass from José López on the left, the ball was threaded back to Julián Álvarez, who had been largely unnoticed until that instant. Álvarez seized the opportunity, unleashing a powerful strike that found the back of the net, leaving the Swiss defense and goalkeeper unable to respond. The goal secured Argentina’s victory and ensured their progression to the next stage of the tournament.

With this win, Argentina has advanced to the semi‑finals, continuing their quest for the World Cup title. The match underscored the unpredictable nature of the competition, as the Argentine side must now navigate another series of high‑pressure encounters to reach the final.
summary: Argentina won 2-1 after Julián Álvarez scored in extra time. The victory sends Argentina into the World Cup semi‑finals.

title: Dutch honeybee winter losses reach 24% in 2025‑2026
content:
In the winter of 2025‑2026, Dutch honeybee colonies suffered a 24 % loss, marking the fourth consecutive year that winter mortality has exceeded 20 %. The data, drawn from the annual survey of beekeepers across the Netherlands, confirm that the upward trend in colony losses seen in recent years has continued.

Regional analysis shows marked variation. The province of Groningen recorded the highest winter loss at 41.5 %, while Overijssel experienced the lowest figure, with only 16.9 % of colonies lost. These disparities highlight the differing environmental and management conditions affecting bee populations across the country.

The sustained high mortality rate underscores the urgent need for targeted interventions and support for beekeepers, as the health of honeybee colonies remains critical for pollination services and agricultural productivity in the Netherlands.
summary: Dutch honeybee winter losses reach 24% in 2025‑2026.
author: Phys.org

title: Synthetic Rotation Mimics Black Hole Energy Extraction in Lab
content: More than half a century ago, Sir Roger Penrose envisioned a scenario in which energy could be extracted from a black hole spinning at extreme speeds. He proposed that a particle entering its ergosphere—a region of space dragged around by a rotating black hole—could split into two. One part could fall into the black hole while the other escaped carrying more energy than the original particle. Building on this theory, physicist Yakov Zel'dovich later predicted that a wave interacting with a sufficiently fast, rotating object could extract energy from it and become amplified.
summary: Scientists have created a laboratory setup that mimics the rotating ergosphere of a black hole, allowing waves to be amplified in a controlled environment. This experiment confirms Zel'dovich’s prediction that rotating objects can extract energy from waves, demonstrating a key aspect of black hole physics.

title: Ant JavaScript runtime and ecosystem launched on Hacker News
content:
A new JavaScript ecosystem called Ant has been unveiled by its author on Hacker News. Ant centers on a custom runtime that ships its own JavaScript engine and is accompanied by a suite of complementary tools: a package manager named the ants, a Land package registry, a deployment and hosting platform, and Ant Desktop for building native desktop applications with web technologies in a manner similar to Electron.

The ecosystem is designed to function as a unified platform while remaining interoperable with the broader JavaScript ecosystem. By integrating these components, Ant aims to provide developers with an end‑to‑end solution for application development, distribution, and deployment without relying on the fragmented stack of existing JavaScript tools. The author notes that the project is still in its early stages and is actively seeking community feedback on its overall direction and the features that would make it a viable alternative to current JavaScript stacks.

Early adopters on Hacker News have expressed interest in the potential of Ant to streamline workflows, though the community has also highlighted the need for robust documentation and clear integration guidelines. The project’s progress will be tracked through its comments and updates on the Hacker News thread, where developers can contribute suggestions and report issues.
summary: The author announced Ant, a JavaScript ecosystem that provides its own runtime, package manager, package registry, deployment platform, and a desktop app builder similar to Electron. The early‑stage project has attracted 70 points and 34 comments on the Hacker News post.

title: Nopia synth near market launch with £550 price tag
content:
Nopia, the hybrid synthesizer unveiled by creators Martin Grieco and Rocío Gal, is poised to hit the market in the coming months. The duo first revealed the device in a 2023 preview that set the online music‑gear community abuzz, and a recent in‑depth look at MusicRadar confirmed that the product will launch for roughly £550. The announcement comes as the pair prepare to transition the prototype from concept to commercial release.

The Nopia is engineered around harmonic interplay rather than a single patch. Its design fuses multiple modules—keys, bass, arpeggiator, and pad—into one cohesive performance, resembling a drum‑less groovebox. A one‑octave “Chord Builder” keyboard and a 12‑note sequencer provide the core of its interface, while the integrated modules allow users to blend sounds in real time without the need for external software. This modular approach gives the instrument a distinctive workflow that differentiates it from conventional synthesizers.

With production slated to begin shortly, the Nopia’s launch represents a notable addition to the boutique synth market. Its hybrid architecture and affordable price point are expected to attract both seasoned producers and newcomers seeking a compact, all‑in‑one solution for live performance and studio work. The Verge will publish the full story, offering a deeper dive into the device’s specifications and the creators’ vision.
summary: The Nopia synthesizer, created by Martin Grieco and Rocío Gal, is almost ready for release and is expected to launch in a few months. It will be priced at around £550 and features a one‑octave Chord Builder keyboard that blends multiple modules for harmonic interplay.

title: South Africa prove too strong for enterprising Scotland in Nations Championship
content:
South Africa Secures Convincing Win Over Scotland in Pretoria

In a high-intensity match played at the high altitude of Pretoria, South Africa emerged victorious over Scotland with a score of 42-28. Despite Scotland's impressive display, scoring four tries and showcasing their pace and skill, the Springboks' sheer power and dominance in the middle of each half ultimately proved decisive. The visitors' tries were spread across the four quarters, with Scotland managing to stay in touch throughout the match.

However, South Africa's unyielding middle game performance allowed them to capitalize on their strength and score five out of six tries during this period. As the match drew to a close, Scotland found themselves within striking distance of a losing bonus point, but a late try from Jesse Kriel sealed the deal for the Springboks. This convincing win sees South Africa march on, while Scotland will look to regroup and improve their performance in their next match.

The match was a testament to the challenges of playing at high altitude, with both teams struggling to cope with the thin air. Nevertheless, South Africa's superior power and physicality ultimately gave them the edge they needed to secure a full house of points. With this win, the Springboks continue to assert their dominance in the competition, leaving Scotland to ponder their next move.
summary: South Africa prove too strong for enterprising Scotland in Nations Championship.

title: Forecast Error Influences Public Emotions During Disasters
content: What happens when weather forecasts do not match reality? How does the public emotionally respond when a disaster unfolds differently from what they expected? A research team led by Professor Jonghun Kam and Kiru Kim from the Department of Environmental Engineering at POSTECH investigated how forecast error types influenced public emotion during the landfall of Typhoon Khanun. Using artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP), the researchers found that different types of forecast error (e. G., overestimation and underestimation) triggered distinct emotional responses among the public. The study has been published in GeoHealth.
summary: A research team led by Professor Jonghun Kam and Kiru Kim studied the impact of forecast errors on public emotions during the landfall of Typhoon Khanun. The study found that different types of forecast errors, such as overestimation and underestimation, triggered distinct emotional responses among the public.

title: Heavy Traffic Makes Flower-Rich Road Verge Dangerous for Bumblebees
content: Flower-rich road verges may attract hungry bumblebees, but at the same time, they can be dangerous for the buzzing insects—if traffic is too heavy. The new research from Lund University in Sweden examined the role roadsides play for bumblebees. The results show that road verges can be a dangerous environment for insects searching for food. The team used specially trained dogs that had learned to sniff out bumblebee nests to assist them. The survey covered 60 road verges in southern Sweden and compared the number of dead and living bumblebees along roads with varying traffic intensities.
summary: A Lund University study examined 60 road verges in southern Sweden and compared bumblebee mortality across different traffic levels. The results showed that higher traffic intensity increased the number of dead bumblebees, making flower-rich verges dangerous for the insects.

title: Plastic Bottle Cap Carries Invasive Species to Japan
content: Researchers have traced the journey of a plastic bottle cap recovered near the waters of southern Japan by combining data from the label, chemical clues in tiny shells and ocean current simulations. They found 307 organisms, including a polychaete worm not found in Japanese waters before. The findings, published in Marine Pollution Bulletin, show that when species that significantly shape their environments (ecosystem engineers) colonize plastic debris, entire micro-communities can be transported over extended periods, with implications for invasive species risk and marine biodiversity conservation.
summary: Researchers have tracked the journey of a plastic bottle cap found near southern Japan, discovering 307 organisms, including a previously unknown species in Japanese waters. The study's findings highlight the potential for plastic debris to transport invasive species and impact marine biodiversity.

summary: Two Asian praying mantis species have been classified as invasive in Europe, where they are rapidly spreading and preying on native insects and small vertebrates. content: Heatwaves have long been part of the Tour but temperatures now are pushing the riders to limit of human enduranceThe Tour de France and the heat of the midday sun are old bedfellows, going back long before an era when the biggest catastrophe of the Tour’s opening week was a major fault in the Visma team bus’s air conditioning. title: Hottap Go Portable Shower Tested for Vanlife and Outdoor Use
content:
A portable shower system that combines a built‑in water reservoir with a compact heating element is gaining attention among outdoor enthusiasts after a series of field tests. The Hottap Go, developed by Australian company Joolca, integrates a 12‑liter water tank directly into the unit, eliminating the need for separate containers and lengthy hoses that have traditionally hampered the practicality of mobile shower solutions. During a recent van‑life itinerary that included surf sessions, campsite cooking, and extended overland travel, the device was evaluated for its ability to deliver consistent hot water in varied conditions, from music‑festival camping to remote backcountry work sites.

Testers reported that the Hottap Go reliably heated water to comfortable temperatures within a few minutes, providing a full shower cycle without the bulk of external tanks. The system’s design allows it to be powered from standard 12‑volt vehicle outlets, and its compact form factor fits easily within limited van storage spaces. While the unit commands a premium price compared to basic portable shower kits, its integrated tank and rapid heating capability position it as a functional alternative for users seeking a more convenient hot‑water experience while on the road.
summary: The author tested the Hottap Go portable shower while vanlifing, surfing, and cooking. It features a 12‑liter integrated water tank and is designed for use in remote locations.

England's ability to contain Haaland will be crucial in determining the outcome of their World Cup encounter.

title: Universe Expansion Acceleration Remains Unexplained
content: For nearly a century, astronomers have known that the universe is expanding. In the late 1990s, two independent teams, the Supernova Cosmology Project, led by Saul Perlmutter, and the High-Z Supernova Search Team, led by Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess, discovered something strange: The expansion is speeding up. The finding earned them the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. The leading explanation for this acceleration is "dark energy," a mysterious force usually modeled as a constant called Lambda, pushing space apart. Combined with cold dark matter, this gives us the LCDM model, the standard picture of the cosmos for the past 25 years.
summary: The universe's expansion is accelerating due to a mysterious force known as dark energy. The discovery of this acceleration was made by two independent teams in the late 1990s and is a key component of the standard LCDM model of the cosmos.

title: New Therapy for Bone Marrow Recovery After Injury
content: A healthy bone marrow (BM) produces nearly all types of cells in our blood. Many blood disorders occur when hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in the BM malfunction. Treatment with radiation or chemotherapy for many blood disorders and cancers can, as a side effect, deplete not only tumor cells but also hematopoietic cells, including HSCs in the BM—a condition known as myelosuppression. In severe cases, HSC transplantation (HSCT) is required to restore hematopoiesis.
summary: A healthy bone marrow produces nearly all types of cells in the blood, including blood cells that are essential for treating blood disorders. Radiation and chemotherapy treatment can cause myelosuppression, a condition where bone marrow is depleted of its ability to produce blood cells.

title: NATO Summit in Ankara Highlights Security Threats and Diplomatic Gifts
content:
The NATO summit in Ankara concluded this week with 32 alliance leaders meeting at the Presidential Compound, and a clearer picture of the event’s behind‑the‑scenes dynamics is now emerging. Reports from The Wall Street Journal and The Times of Israel indicate that President Trump’s team was rapidly adjusting their agenda in response to an alleged Iranian assassination threat, a development that unfolded largely outside the main plenary sessions.

Side meetings also shaped the summit’s agenda. Baltic leaders met with President Volodymyr Zelensky to discuss regional security, while Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan presented ceremonial pistols with ammunition to visiting dignitaries—a gesture that sparked a diplomatic and ethical debate over whether such gifts should be accepted. These incidents illustrate the complex interplay of security concerns and diplomatic protocols that accompanied the formal NATO discussions.

French‑based broadcaster France 24’s Gavin Lee spoke with Joakim Klementi, European correspondent for Estonian Public Broadcasting (ERR), who provided additional context on the summit’s side meetings and the diplomatic tensions surrounding Erdoğan’s gifts. The event’s final day underscored the multifaceted nature of NATO’s collective security efforts amid ongoing geopolitical pressures.
summary: The NATO summit in Ankara involved 32 leaders and included discussions on an Iranian assassination threat that prompted adjustments by President Trump's team. Side meetings saw Baltic leaders discuss matters with President Zelensky, while Turkish President Erdogan's ceremonial pistol gifts raised diplomatic concerns.
author: France 24

title: Exoplanet LHS 3844b's Extreme Day-Night Cycle
content: Ever so slightly bigger than Earth, the exoplanet LHS 3844b orbits its parent star, LHS 3844, a red dwarf 48.5 light-years from our solar system. Its rotational speed mirrors its orbital speed. The result? One side of LHS 3844b is perpetually bathed in scorching sunlight, locked into a never-ending, blistering hot day, while the other is forever shrouded in darkness so cold that particles are incapable of movement, a state known as absolute zero (zero Kelvin).
summary: LHS 3844b, an exoplanet slightly larger than Earth, orbits a red dwarf star 48.5 light-years from our solar system. The exoplanet's extreme day-night cycle results in one side experiencing constant sunlight and the other side perpetual darkness.

title: England players praise Thomas Tuchel's leadership at the World Cup
content: Imposing head coach is a details man who has got the balance of squad spirit right at the World Cup, and is even proving a hit on MumsnetLet’s set the world on fire. There’s a section in Bill Buford’s classic football hooligan study, Among the Thugs, where he describes being part of a phalanx of England “faces” steaming through the centre of mid-1980s Rotterdam towards some kind of meet, while their leader – the Top Boy, General or similar – runs up and down the column whispering to his men, saying the “energy is high”, “the energy is high”, “feel it”, “the energy is high”. As it is currently for this England team, and quite clearly the players can feel it. You will probably have seen the dressing-room video, which has more than 40m views. Declan Rice and John Stones are shown playing a prank on Thomas Tuchel after the electrical storm masquerading as a football match at the Estadio Azteca on Sunday. Rice pretends Stones has injured his shoulder. Stones plays along with it, delivering a minimalist acting masterclass so contained there is almost no acting at all, before raising his fist as the beat drops (song: Talk To You, by ANOTR) and the room falls about in generalised hysteria. title: Politically charged immigration issues linked to increased industrial pollution

The research team describes this phenomenon as "institutional crowding."
summary: A joint research study led by Professor Narae Lee from KAIST and Professor Heli Wang from Singapore Management University found that immigration-related legislation can lead to weaker government environmental oversight. The study found a correlation between politically salient immigration issues and increased industrial pollution in the United States.

title: Study suggests Mount Etna may represent a new type of volcano
content: Mount Etna has long puzzled geologists because it doesn't fit any of the three classic ways volcanoes are thought to form. A new study suggests it may instead be fueled by ancient pockets of magma that are pushed upward through cracks created by shifting tectonic plates. If confirmed, Etna could belong to a rare fourth category of volcano, revealing that much larger volcanoes can form through processes previously associated only with small submarine eruptions.
summary: A new study proposes that Mount Etna’s activity is driven by ancient magma pockets forced upward through cracks created by shifting tectonic plates. If confirmed, Etna would belong to a rare fourth category of volcano, showing that large volcanoes can form by processes previously associated only with small submarine eruptions.

title: Mayo Clinic Expert Links Heart Health to Brain Health to Reduce Alzheimer's Risk
content: The same lifestyle choices that reduce your risk of heart disease, diabetes and cancer can also reduce your risk of cognitive decline. Bryan Woodruff, M. D., a cognitive neurologist at Mayo Clinic in Arizona, explains the brain-body connection, lifestyle changes to foster brain health, and why work to make earlier detection of Alzheimer's disease and other dementias is important.

title: Dengue Spread in Europe Fueled by Aedes albopictus Mosquitoes
content: Dengue is caused by the dengue virus and transmitted by mosquito bites. Traditionally endemic in tropical regions such as Latin America and the Caribbean, as well as Southeast Asia, local transmission across several countries in mainland Europe has been documented since 2010. In particular, the mosquito species Aedes albopictus, which is now well established in southern Europe, can act as a dengue vector even though the main dengue vector is Aedes aegypti.
summary: Dengue, transmitted by mosquito bites, has been locally transmitted in several mainland European countries since 2010. The well-established Aedes albopictus mosquito in southern Europe can act as a dengue vector, even though the primary vector is Aedes aegypti.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Meningococcal B vaccine shows no effect on gonorrhea rates in MSM, RCT finds
content: The meningococcal B vaccine is ineffective in gonorrhea prevention among men who have sex with men (MSM) at high risk of infection, according to findings from the world's largest randomized controlled trial (RCT) into possible efficacy published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Contrary to evidence in observational studies that led to vaccination programs abroad, GoGoVax found that 4CMenB (meningococcal B vaccine) had no effect on the incidence of gonorrhea.
summary: The world's largest randomized controlled trial found that the 4CMenB meningococcal B vaccine did not reduce gonorrhea incidence among high‑risk men who have sex with men. This result contrasts with earlier observational studies that had suggested a protective effect and may affect vaccination program decisions.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study Finds Geriatric Patients Can Use Digital Nutrition Apps With Age-Appropriate Design
content: In an era where digital health applications are booming, older adults, particularly those facing the physical and psychological toll of post-acute rehabilitation, are frequently left out of the equation because of assumptions about low-tech literacy. However, a prospective pilot study published in JMIR Aging shows that with age-appropriate design, even clinically burdened geriatric patients can independently use mobile apps to manage their nutrition.
summary: A prospective pilot study published in JMIR Aging found that older adults, even those with clinical burdens, can independently use mobile nutrition apps when the apps are designed for their age group. The study indicates that age-appropriate design enables geriatric patients to manage their nutrition digitally.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Food Insecurity Drives Telehealth Abortion Choice
content: Individuals seeking abortion face considerable challenges, including high costs, logistical difficulties such as travel and dependent care, and fear of stigma. In recent years, access to care has improved through telehealth abortion-related medical care via video consultations and phone calls, with medication delivered by mail, along with pre-abortion counseling. This increasingly used care option is patient-centered and is comparably safe and effective as in-person care. However, the factors that guide patient selection of telehealth abortion remain uncertain.
summary: A study found that individuals facing food insecurity are more likely to choose telehealth abortion services. The research suggests that financial and logistical barriers, including lack of food security, influence the decision to use remote medical abortion.

title: Australian Study Shows Donated Breast Milk Reduces NEC by 38%
content: The rate of a life-threatening gut disease called necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) has decreased by 38% in very premature babies who received donated breast milk from Australian Red Cross Lifeblood, according to research published in the Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health. The study is the first in Australia to look at the benefits and risks of donated breast milk for very preterm babies born less than 32 weeks.
summary: The study found a 38% reduction in necrotizing enterocolitis among very premature infants who received donated breast milk. It is the first Australian research to evaluate the benefits and risks of donated breast milk for babies born before 32 weeks.

title: Study finds 96% drop in morning glories' adaptation rate as pollinator pressure rises
content:
A University of Michigan research team has found that plants facing simultaneous pressures from climate change and a collapsing pollinator population may be prioritizing traits that attract pollinators over those that confer heat tolerance. The trade‑off, observed in a nine‑year study of morning glories, resulted in a 96 percent reduction in the species’ overall rate of adaptation, suggesting that the evolutionary response to warming temperatures is being compromised.

The decline in adaptive capacity could have practical implications for agriculture, as morning glories are considered a nuisance crop by many farmers. The findings, which appear in the journal Evolution Letters, highlight the potential for reduced plant resilience in changing ecosystems and underscore the interconnected challenges posed by climate stressors and pollinator loss.
summary: University of Michigan researchers observed a 96% decrease in the rate of adaptation of morning glory populations over nine years. The findings, published in Evolution Letters, link the decline to heightened pollinator pressure amid climate change and note potential implications for farmers who consider the plant a nuisance.

title: Study finds religious songs and drums strengthen transnational Matua community
content: Professor Carola Lorea of the University of Tübingen's Department of Social and Cultural Anthropology has published a comprehensive academic study on the Matua, a community of 50 million people scattered across India, Bangladesh and 32 other nations in the wake of evictions and forced migration. Despite national borders and natural barriers such as the Bay of Bengal Delta, swamps and the sea, the community's cohesion has only grown over the decades. Lorea's work represents more than 10 years of field studies into Matua life, and she describes how religious songs, drum rhythms and shared stories play a vital role in Matua society and have even made a protest movement possible.
summary: Study finds religious songs and drums strengthen transnational Matua community.

title: Physicists demonstrate emergent time in ultracold atom quantum system
content: What if time doesn't actually exist until something changes? Scientists at the University of Birmingham created a tiny "mini universe" using 24,000 ultracold atoms and showed that the flow of time can emerge naturally from changes inside a quantum system, without relying on any external clock.

Their laboratory model suggests these worlds may be more hospitable than previously thought, despite their extreme surface conditions.
summary: Researchers modeled a tidally locked exoplanet and discovered that internal heat can circulate in a stable, continuous loop. The model indicates that this heat transport could moderate temperatures in certain regions, allowing the planet to potentially support life despite permanent day and night sides.
